title: Bedside interpretation: ECG, CXR, CT and labs
summary: Bedside interpretation for the ICU: systematic ECG reading and troponin, chest X-ray device and lung patterns, CT head indications and reading, liver, coagulation and cardiac biomarkers, and microbiology results.

topics.title: ECG interpretation in the ICU
topics.summary: A systematic 12-lead read, STEMI criteria and their mimics, troponin in critical illness, QTc risk and electrolyte patterns.

definition.text: Use a fixed sequence for every ECG: rate, rhythm, axis, intervals (PR, QRS, QTc), P waves, QRS morphology, ST segments, T waves, and comparison with previous tracings. In the ICU most troponin rises are myocardial injury or type 2 MI rather than type 1 (plaque rupture) MI.

steps.title: Rate and rhythm
steps.detail: Regular or irregular; P before every QRS; narrow vs broad complex (see cardiac-emergencies-arrhythmias module for management).

steps.title: Intervals
steps.detail: PR 120-200 ms; QRS < 120 ms; QTc (Bazett, or Fridericia when HR > 100): > 500 ms or rise > 60 ms from baseline = high torsades risk.

steps.title: ST elevation (STEMI)
steps.detail: New ST elevation at the J point in ≥ 2 contiguous leads: ≥ 1 mm in all leads except V2-V3, where ≥ 2 mm (men ≥ 40 y), ≥ 2.5 mm (men < 40 y), ≥ 1.5 mm (women).

steps.title: STEMI equivalents
steps.detail: Posterior MI (ST depression V1-V3, tall R; check V7-V9), new LBBB with ischaemic symptoms or Sgarbossa criteria, de Winter T waves, diffuse ST depression with aVR elevation (left main / multivessel ischaemia).

steps.title: Mimics
steps.detail: Pericarditis (diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression), LV aneurysm, early repolarisation, hyperkalaemia, Brugada, Takotsubo, raised ICP (deep T inversion).

steps.title: Troponin
steps.detail: Above the 99th percentile with a rise/fall = myocardial injury; MI requires ischaemic symptoms, ECG changes, imaging or angiographic evidence. Sepsis, PE, tachyarrhythmia, AKI and shock cause type 2 MI or non-ischaemic injury.

steps.title: Electrolytes
steps.detail: Hyperkalaemia: peaked T → PR prolongation, P loss → broad QRS → sine wave. Hypokalaemia: U waves, ST depression. Hypocalcaemia: long QT. Hypercalcaemia: short QT.

tables.title: Common ICU drugs that prolong QT
tables.caption: Stop QT-prolonging drugs and correct K (to 4-5 mmol/L) and Mg when QTc > 500 ms.

redFlags.text: STEMI or STEMI-equivalent in an ICU patient: immediate cardiology discussion for reperfusion even if the admission diagnosis was non-cardiac.
QTc > 500 ms with bradycardia, hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia: high risk of torsades.

pitfalls.text: Labelling every troponin rise in sepsis as 'NSTEMI' and starting dual antiplatelets.
Machine QTc in AF, bundle branch block or with wide U waves - measure manually.

pearls.text: Always compare with the previous ECG - new changes matter more than absolute values.

algorithm.title: Troponin rise in an ICU patient

nodes.text: Ischaemic symptoms, new wall motion abnormality or new ischaemic ECG changes?
Type 1 vs type 2 MI: echo; treat supply-demand cause (shock, anaemia, tachyarrhythmia, hypoxaemia)
Acute non-ischaemic myocardial injury: treat cause (sepsis, PE, myocarditis)
Cardiology review: antithrombotic plan and angiography decision

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Critical illness raises myocardial oxygen demand (tachycardia, catecholamines) and reduces supply (hypotension, anaemia, hypoxaemia), causing type 2 MI; direct injury comes from sepsis, myocarditis, PE (RV strain) and toxins.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- Fourth universal definition of MI [Thygesen 2018].
- ESC 2023 ACS guideline: STEMI criteria and equivalents [Byrne 2023].
- AHA/ACCF 2010 statement on torsades prevention in hospital [Drew 2010].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Benefit of coronary angiography for type 2 MI; QT correction formula at high heart rates.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Indian patients present with ACS at younger ages; STEMI equivalents in ICU are under-recognised.
- High-sensitivity troponin assays and cut-offs differ by laboratory - always use the local 99th percentile.

topics.title: Chest X-ray in the ICU: lines, tubes and lung patterns
topics.summary: Checking devices on supine films, recognising ARDS, oedema, pneumothorax and effusion, and when ultrasound beats the X-ray.

definition.text: The ICU portable (AP supine) film is mainly for device position and gross pathology; it underestimates effusions and pneumothoraces. Bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion, collapse or nodules are part of the ARDS definition (CXR, CT or lung ultrasound under the 2023 global definition).

steps.title: Check the film
steps.detail: Patient, date, AP/PA, supine/erect, rotation (clavicle heads vs spinous processes), inspiration.

steps.title: Endotracheal tube
steps.detail: Tip 3-7 cm above the carina (about T2-T4, between clavicle heads); head flexion moves the tip down, extension up.

steps.title: Central venous catheter
steps.detail: Tip at the lower SVC / cavo-atrial junction (about at or just below the carina); check for loops, crossing into the contralateral subclavian or the azygos vein; exclude pneumothorax.

steps.title: Nasogastric tube
steps.detail: Follows midline down the oesophagus, bisects the carina, crosses the diaphragm and the tip lies below the left hemidiaphragm in the stomach; never feed if uncertain.

steps.title: Other devices
steps.detail: Chest drain side hole inside the pleura; IABP tip 2-3 cm below the top of the aortic arch (aortic knob); pacing wire in the RV apex.

steps.title: Lungs
steps.detail: ARDS: bilateral opacities, often peripheral, normal heart size; cardiogenic oedema: upper-lobe diversion, septal lines, perihilar 'bat-wing', effusions, cardiomegaly; pneumonia: lobar consolidation with air bronchograms.

steps.title: Pleura on a supine film
steps.detail: Pneumothorax: deep sulcus sign, hyperlucent hemithorax; effusion: hazy veil over the hemithorax with preserved vascular markings.

steps.title: Use ultrasound
steps.detail: Lung ultrasound detects pneumothorax (absent sliding, lung point), effusion and B-lines more accurately than a supine CXR.

tables.title: Device position targets
rows: Contralateral subclavian, IJ loop, too deep in RA
Below left hemidiaphragm, ≥ 10 cm into stomach

redFlags.text: NG tube in a bronchus on X-ray: remove before any feed is given.
Deep sulcus sign in a ventilated patient with hypotension: tension pneumothorax until proven otherwise.

pitfalls.text: Accepting radiology of a different tube position after repositioning without a repeat check.
Diagnosing ARDS without excluding cardiogenic oedema (echo).

pearls.text: The 2023 global ARDS definition allows SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 315 (with SpO₂ ≤ 97%) and lung ultrasound for bilateral opacities - useful where ABG or CT is limited.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: In supine films, air rises anteriorly and fluid layers posteriorly, so pneumothoraces appear as basal lucency and effusions as diffuse haze. Magnification of the heart (AP projection) limits assessment of cardiomegaly.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- New global definition of ARDS [Matthay 2024].
- ASA 2020 on catheter tip confirmation [ASA 2020]; BTS 2023 on pleural imaging [Roberts 2023].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Routine daily CXR in ventilated patients (on-demand imaging is as safe in trials and reduces cost).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Portable X-ray availability and quality vary; lung ultrasound is a cheap, radiation-free supplement.
- The global ARDS definition was designed to include resource-limited settings, relevant to many Indian ICUs.

topics.title: CT head: when to scan and how to read it
topics.summary: Indications after head injury, a systematic read (blood, cisterns, brain, ventricles, bone), and early stroke and herniation signs.

definition.text: Non-contrast CT is the first-line brain imaging in the ICU for trauma, sudden neurological deterioration, suspected stroke and before LP when indicated. Read systematically: Blood, Cisterns, Brain, Ventricles, Bone ('Blood Can Be Very Bad').

steps.title: Head injury - scan within 1 h (NICE)
steps.detail: GCS < 13 on initial assessment, GCS < 15 at 2 h, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, signs of basal skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, focal deficit, more than 1 episode of vomiting.

steps.title: Anticoagulated patients
steps.detail: Head injury on anticoagulants: CT within 8 h even without other risk factors (sooner if other criteria).

steps.title: Blood
steps.detail: Hyperdense (acute blood 50-100 HU): extradural (lentiform, crosses no sutures), subdural (crescentic, crosses sutures), subarachnoid (in sulci/cisterns), intraparenchymal, intraventricular.

steps.title: Cisterns
steps.detail: Effaced basal cisterns (perimesencephalic) suggest raised ICP and herniation risk.

steps.title: Brain
steps.detail: Grey-white differentiation loss, insular ribbon sign, hyperdense MCA sign (early ischaemia); midline shift; oedema.

steps.title: Ventricles
steps.detail: Hydrocephalus (temporal horn dilatation), effacement from mass effect, intraventricular blood.

steps.title: Bone
steps.detail: Fractures on bone windows; air in the cranium (pneumocephalus) suggests open or basal fracture.

steps.title: Stroke
steps.detail: Non-contrast CT excludes haemorrhage before thrombolysis; ASPECTS scores early MCA ischaemia; CT angiography for large-vessel occlusion if thrombectomy is possible.

tables.title: CT patterns and action
rows: Neurosurgery if thick, shift, or deteriorating

redFlags.text: Falling GCS with a new dilated pupil: treat as herniation (osmotherapy, brief hyperventilation) and arrange immediate CT and neurosurgery.

pitfalls.text: Reading only the brain window - always review bone and subdural windows.
A normal early CT does not exclude ischaemic stroke, diffuse axonal injury or encephalitis.

pearls.text: Isodense subacute subdurals (about 1-3 weeks) are easily missed - look for sulcal effacement and midline shift.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: CT density depends on haemoglobin concentration: acute clot is bright, then becomes isodense and later hypodense; ischaemic oedema reduces density progressively over hours.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- NICE NG232 head injury guideline [NICE 2023]; Canadian CT Head Rule [Stiell 2001].
- AHA/ASA 2019 stroke guideline for imaging pathways [Powers 2019].
consultantNotes.controversies: - CT for minor head injury in elderly anticoagulated patients; routine repeat CT in stable traumatic bleeds.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Road traffic injuries are the commonest cause of head injury in India; CT access may require transfer - stabilise and follow transport safety rules (handover-transport module).
- Thrombolysis-capable stroke units are expanding but uneven; know the nearest thrombectomy centre.

topics.title: Liver tests, coagulation and cardiac biomarkers
topics.summary: Patterns of LFT derangement, ischaemic hepatitis, interpreting PT/INR, fibrinogen and DIC scores, natriuretic peptides, lactate and procalcitonin.

definition.text: ICU labs are best interpreted as patterns and trends. LFT patterns are classified by the R ratio [(ALT/ULN)/(ALP/ULN)]: ≥ 5 hepatocellular, ≤ 2 cholestatic, 2-5 mixed.

steps.title: LFT pattern
steps.detail: Calculate R ratio; ALT > 1,000 units/L suggests ischaemic hepatitis, paracetamol or acute viral hepatitis; cholestasis in ICU is often sepsis, drugs or PN.

steps.title: Ischaemic hepatitis
steps.detail: Very high ALT/AST with high LDH (ALT/LDH < 1.5) after shock, peaking at 1-3 days and falling rapidly.

steps.title: Synthetic function
steps.detail: INR, albumin and bilirubin reflect liver function; INR in cirrhosis does not predict bleeding (see liver-coagulopathy topic).

steps.title: Coagulation
steps.detail: Prolonged PT/APTT: dilution, consumption (DIC), liver failure, vitamin K deficiency, anticoagulants, heparin contamination of samples; check fibrinogen and platelets; viscoelastic tests where available.

steps.title: DIC score (ISTH)
steps.detail: Calculate in a patient with a disorder associated with DIC; ≥ 5 = overt DIC; repeat daily.

steps.title: Natriuretic peptides
steps.detail: Acute heart failure unlikely if NT-proBNP < 300 pg/mL or BNP < 100 pg/mL; values rise with AKI, age, sepsis and PE; lower in obesity.

steps.title: Lactate
steps.detail: Elevated lactate (> 2 mmol/L) marks hypoperfusion or impaired clearance; follow trends to guide resuscitation.

steps.title: Procalcitonin
steps.detail: Do not use PCT to decide whether to start antibiotics in suspected sepsis; use PCT with clinical review to support stopping antibiotics.

tables.title: LFT patterns
rows: Ischaemic hepatitis, paracetamol, viral (hepatitis A/E, dengue), drugs
Sepsis cholestasis, biliary obstruction, PN, drugs (co-amoxiclav, ceftriaxone sludge)

redFlags.text: Rising INR with encephalopathy in a patient without cirrhosis: acute liver failure - contact a liver centre (liver-failure module).

pitfalls.text: Treating an abnormal INR with FFP in a non-bleeding patient before a low-risk procedure.
Starting or continuing antibiotics because of a single PCT value.

pearls.text: Isolated high unconjugated bilirubin in ICU: consider haemolysis (LDH, haptoglobin, smear) and large haematoma resorption.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Hepatocyte necrosis releases transaminases; cholestasis raises ALP and GGT. In sepsis, cytokines impair bile transport. Consumptive coagulopathy depletes platelets and fibrinogen while fibrin breakdown raises D-dimer.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- ACG 2017 abnormal liver chemistry guideline [Kwo 2017].
- ISTH DIC score [Taylor 2001]; ESC 2021 HF natriuretic peptide thresholds [McDonagh 2021].
- SSC 2026 on lactate (measure and trend) and procalcitonin (not to decide starting; with clinical review to decide stopping) [Prescott 2026]; SAPS PCT-guided discontinuation trial [de Jong 2016].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Lactate as a perfusion target vs capillary refill time; troponin and BNP prognostication in sepsis.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Dengue, leptospirosis, malaria, scrub typhus and hepatitis E commonly cause raised transaminases in Indian ICUs (tropical-monsoon-fevers module).
- PCT is costly; reserve it for stewardship decisions about stopping antibiotics.

topics.title: Cultures and microbiology interpretation
topics.summary: Blood culture technique, contaminants vs true pathogens, respiratory and urine samples, rapid diagnostics and reading an antibiogram.

definition.text: Microbiology results are only as good as the sample: take cultures before antibiotics when this causes no meaningful delay, use correct volume and technique, and interpret the organism in the clinical context.

steps.title: Blood cultures
steps.detail: At least 2 sets (aerobic + anaerobic bottles) from separate venepunctures, 20 mL per set in adults; before antibiotics if no significant delay.

steps.title: Suspected line infection
steps.detail: Paired cultures from the catheter and a peripheral vein; catheter culture positive ≥ 2 h earlier than peripheral (differential time to positivity) suggests catheter-related bacteraemia.

steps.title: Contaminants vs pathogens
steps.detail: Coagulase-negative staphylococci, Corynebacterium, Bacillus (non-anthracis) or Cutibacterium in a single set usually = contamination; S. aureus, Gram-negative bacilli, Candida or S. pneumoniae in any bottle = true bacteraemia.

steps.title: Respiratory samples
steps.detail: Endotracheal aspirate (semi-quantitative) or BAL; Candida in respiratory samples is almost always colonisation.

steps.title: Urine
steps.detail: Culture only with symptoms or sepsis without another source; from the sampling port of a freshly replaced catheter if in situ > 2 weeks.

steps.title: Rapid diagnostics
steps.detail: Rapid identification/resistance tests on positive blood cultures (e.g. multiplex PCR, carbapenemase detection) speed targeted therapy; interpret with stewardship input.

steps.title: Antibiogram
steps.detail: Read MICs against breakpoints (S, I/SDD, R); use the local unit antibiogram for empirical choices and the isolate report for targeted therapy.

tables.title: Positive blood culture: first response
rows: Treat; repeat cultures; echo; ID consult; source control
Review empirical cover against local resistance; source control
Repeat cultures if prosthetic material or line infection suspected

redFlags.text: S. aureus or Candida in a blood culture is never a contaminant - start appropriate therapy and look for a source.

pitfalls.text: A single blood culture set - lower sensitivity and impossible to judge contaminants.
Treating Candida in sputum or asymptomatic bacteriuria.

pearls.text: Underfilled bottles are the commonest reason for false-negative blood cultures - blood volume matters more than timing with fever spikes.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Bacteraemia is often low-grade (< 1 CFU/mL), so sensitivity depends on volume; skin flora contaminate when antisepsis or technique is poor.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- IDSA/ASM 2024 guide to microbiology laboratory use [Miller 2024].
- SSC 2026: blood cultures as soon as possible, ideally before antimicrobials (strong); a single set is acceptable where resources are limited; pathogen-specific rapid tests case by case [Prescott 2026].
- ICMR AMRSN surveillance data on Indian resistance [ICMR 2023].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Routine surveillance cultures in ICU; molecular panels on direct samples versus culture.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Automated blood culture systems are available in most tertiary hospitals but not in many district hospitals; rapid carbapenemase tests (e.g. mCIM, lateral flow) are increasingly used in India and guide choice between ceftazidime-avibactam ± aztreonam and polymyxins.
- High CRE/CRAB rates (ICMR AMRSN) mean the local antibiogram must be updated at least yearly.
